Actually this is incorrect. All the Australian constitution says is that you have to report to the polls on a election. They don't care whether you bother to vote or just draw a picture of a penis on your ballot - that is vote informally. You are not "forced" to vote for anyone and doing so would be impossible to enforce anyway.

Also, interestingly enough, you have preference voting where you number the candidates in in order. So if you choose to vote for a third party then you don't automatically throw your vote away - in a loose summary. You can argue whether this is a good or a bad thing. For example it's good in that it gives third parties an actual chance but bad in that it makes the process that much more complex. And so on and so forth.

In addition to that they use a parliamentary system under a constitutional monarchy. So when you vote you're not really directly voting for the Prime Minister but rather the local representative. For example just before the last election the party that was in power at the time didn't like their chances with the guy they had running the show so they just got rid of him and put someone else in power. Outside of polling the general public doesn't really get a say as to how gets to run the country. Hell they're not even privy to when it's put to a vote at a party caucus.

The closest office to that of President in Australia would be the Governor General who is supposed to be the Queen's representative in Australia. Basically it's exactly like Canada where the British Queen is also their Queen. While in principle they have ultimate executive power it's more of a symbolic role - but they have used their power to dissolve paraliment before specifically in the mid 70s due to the loans affair. What happens is that the Parliament just decides on some idiot that they what to put into this roll. I doubt that most Australians even know who the current GG is. If this sounds really stupid and antiquated to have a foreign monarch in control of your country then it's probably because it is. It is what it is - and fuck trying to change things.

And there are also two houses. But unlike America power is mainly concentrated in the lower house while the Australian Senate doesn't really do much outside of block, ehm, I mean, provide legislative oversight. As well as seperate state and federal government branches.

To be honest it's a bit of a frogat as to which system you think is better. They both seem based upon the idea of looking like they're doing something while essentially fuck all gets done. IMHO. You still have all the same bullshit of your vote being more or less powerful depending in where you live. That is if you live in a safe seat then forget about the other party bothering to send someone who's actually any good. And you still have a mostly two party system although technicaly one of the main parties - The Liberials - is supposed to be in coalition with another party - The Nationals.

I think that the basic difference seems to be that in parliamentary system parties are loads more powerful then they are in America. For example while it's possible for a member of Parliament to draft a bill - what is called a private members bill - by custom this is normally only used as a device by the opposition to attack the current party in power. Whereas in America anyone can draft a bill but to actually get anything passed is a pretty painful process, for sure. Especially when this comes to all the negotiations between the various political branches of State, House, Senate and President.

If you want to know the actual policies then things are pretty left wing. Eg you have things like universal heath care via a public option, public funding of degrees, high minimum wages etc. The main party in power who are usually the ones that are, The Liberials, are supposed to be the conservative party but even they are probably far to the left of what the Democrats are in America. Although they're probably still slightly to the right of European parties.
